lines.text: Our robot has to drop this piece within two centimeters. About the width of your thumb.
Easy: drive to where the map says. But real fields are built by people, so the target is a few centimeters off.
So near the end, the robot stops trusting the map. It reads the target's own AprilTag and measures where it really is.
But every photo is a little old. By then, the robot moved about five centimeters. So it remembers where its wheels were when the photo was taken.
A camera turned just one degree sees the tag almost two centimeters off. So each camera is calibrated once, on the real spot.
Now, the drive. A robot that slows down only when it's close overshoots. Ours asks fifty times a second: can I still stop?
And it never asks the tires for more than they can grip. Speeding up shifts weight back, so the front wheels slip first.
Measure the target. Rewind the photo. Fix the camera. Brake on time. Respect the tires.
That's how a robot hits a two-centimeter target.
